doc.title: Ed Polcer interviewed by Monk Rowe, Tarrytown, New York, October 31, 1998

title: Getting discovered at Princeton by Dennis Brady and Stan Rubin
summary: He played records loudly from his dorm window and was recruited by Dennis Brady's Nassau Jazz Band. Stan Rubin then brought them to Carnegie Hall and took him on a European student ship.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: I read an interesting anecdote of yours about when you went to Princeton, you wanted to get in on the jazz scene.
How I pushed to be discovered.

It was like story book. I mean I didn’t know Princeton and the Ivy League tradition and anything like that. I mean I was never caught up in it. I never thought I’d go to an Ivy League school. We couldn’t afford it. So it was never a thing. All I knew is when I was a kid Dick Hasmeier played football and was all-American and played, and that was Princeton. And every Saturday when I was in high school, Ted Huesing, the radio disc jockey, had a thing called, well he had “Ted Heusing’s Bandstand” on WNEW or WINS radio, and for an hour every Saturday morning he’d feature Dixieland or traditional jazz. And every once in a while he would feature Stan Rubin and his Tigertown Five. And Stan was the class of ‘55, 1955 at Princeton, I was the class of ‘58. And by the time I got this scholarship and decided to go to Princeton I said I’d love to work with Stan Rubin. He was still there. He was a senior when I was a freshman. So freshman week, I was in my dorm, I opened the window up, turned on, we called them “hi-fi’s” in those days, and

was playing a Dixieland jazz thing and playing very hot, saying somebody’s going to hear me. And the first time I tried this, I wasn’t doing it for more than about a half an hour and suddenly I get a knock on the door. It wasn’t Stan Rubin, but it was one of his competitors, Dennis Brady, who had the Nassau Jazz Band, and it took that long for him to ask me to become his cornet player. Stan Rubin heard us, Stan Rubin booked us in Carnegie Hall along with his band, he had the Nassau Jazz Band play a couple of tunes because we were his discovery, and Stan would hire all the greats, I mean, of the traditional era: Max Kaminsky, Buck Clayton, people like that, and they’d each do a set and it would finish off with Stan Rubin and his Tigertown Five. And then the next year Stan went to play at Grace Kelly’s wedding, and his regular trumpet player wanted to get paid more money for the job and refused to go, so Stan called me and said do you want to go, and that was — actually the summer before that Stan booked us on a Holland America line ship where we went to Europe, we played on a student ship and came back, so I had a tour of Europe after my freshman year of college. So I was welcomed into the jazz community very nicely, I had all the ups and none of the downs at that point.
Were your tastes changing at all as you went along? Let’s say by the time you graduated you were in your early 20s. Your tastes pretty much stayed with the traditional jazz at that time?
